messages.subject: STAN Posterior sampling question
parts:
Hi guys,

To jump straight into it, I was wondering if someone could explain to make why the sampled posterior region of STAN appears to be close to a normal, instead of sampling proportionally to the posterior. To motivate this, I wrote my whole STAN model such that I have a variable Posterior which is calculated in the the transformed parameters section of the model, with the final model simply being:

data {
    ...
}
transformed data {
    ...
}
parameters {
    ...
}
transformed parameters {
    ...
    approximate_efficiency = ...
    Posterior = stuff - approximate_efficiency
}
model {
    target += Posterior;
}

Thus I get the logposterior values (up to a constant) out of stan, and plotting this gives the figure below (x-axis is just the step index). I am seeking to understand why the distribution looks like it does, or to find out if I have made a mistake in my thinking.


To go into more detail, I been using STAN to try and do some cosmology fitting for my PhD. It's going well, but I am still very new to STAN and to Bayesian methods in general. There is one part of the model which is too complicated to be implemented in STAN (have to do MC integration instead), and so I have implemented an approximation in STAN, and then reweight the STAN chains afterwards to adjust for the difference between the approximate correction and the actual correction (the approximate weight (ie efficiency) is recorded by stan, so I can reweight after the fact by weighting each step by approximate_efficiency - actual_efficiency) . Now here is where it gets interesting - when I change the approximation my posterior surfaces shift - and this should not be happening because mathematically the approximation cancels out, because its contribution in STAN is removed in the reweighting. In my bid to understand what is going on, I think I first need to understand why the samples are distributed as they are in logposterior space.

Any help, thoughts or explanations would be greatly appreciated!

Hi,

A couple quick comments first. Then some stuff inline:
- Stan is "Stan," not "STAN." It's a name (named after Stanislaw Ulam), not an acronym.
- it's really hard to help when you don't provide working code. Ideally, you can provide a small example, but just indicating you have a problem and the skeleton of the program doesn't make it any easier to identify if it's a coding error, a misspecification of the model, or even a bug in Stan. Think about writing for someone else to read. Being concise while providing as much context is good. Providing something that can be verified and discussed is better. 

I think that second point is going to prevent a lot of people jumping in to help. Perhaps you can provide a simple, complete example?

Hi guys,

To jump straight into it, I was wondering if someone could explain to make why the sampled posterior region of STAN appears to be close to a normal, instead of sampling proportionally to the posterior.

If using the default algorithm, the draws should be from the posterior distribution. In Stan, you're specifying the log joint probability distribution function (not the posterior -- the joint lpdf is proportional to the posterior distribution). 

Why do you think the draws are "close to a normal"? (What does "close to" mean in this context?) And what tells you that the posterior shouldn't be? (Can't tell based on the program provided)

Hi Daniel,

Thanks for the heads up about the name, Im used to just assuming the acronym!

And I understand about providing a code example, at the moment I don't have a smaller reproduction, just the full model found at https://github.com/dessn/sn-bhm/blob/master/dessn/models/d_simple_stan/approx_mass/model.stan (but Ill try and create a toy example, because I dont expect anyone to go through that big model). As to what I am unable to put into stan, it is a high dimensional integral that appears on the denominator of the likelihood, not the numerator, so the standard way of marginalising over parameters doesn't won't work. If there is a way to put a theta-dependent integral on the denominator of the joint lpdf I would be very happy to break free of my ignorance!

I will create a toy model asap and update this post with it, but in the meantime perhaps I can make my enquiry about the joint lpdf distribution clearer. 

The plot I included is just a trace plot of the joint lpdf (what I called the posterior) subtracted from the max value of the joint lpdf. It is sorted by another parameter (which is responsible for the trend). What I was inquiring about was the distribution of the points. For example, if the chains from Stan are equally weighted, it seems that it has sampled points with a joint lpdf of around -200 far more than points which have a joint lpdf between 0 and -100. This is confusing to me, as I thought the higher the joint lpdf, the more samples one should get. Does that make my confusion/position any easier to understand?

Thank you for reading through so far, I'll try and get smaller examples working as quickly as I can!

Yes. And it's what you want. Stan's MCMC *samples* from the posterior,
it doesn't optimize it.

Here's a simple example you can recreate in R without Stan using
only simple Monte Carlo sampling. Suppose you have bernoulli(0.7)
and you draw 100 samples. Most of those samples are going
to have around 70 successes in them even though 100 successes
had *much* higher probability.

For instance, 50 replication of 100 draws with a 70% chance of
success.

> rbinom(50, 100, 0.7)
[1] 65 79 66 75 73 69 63 69 73 71 68 72 65 77 68 73 64 71 61 68 76 72 75 72 74
[26] 78 65 67 72 65 67 69 63 76 76 70 72 75 72 69 66 71 75 66 70 62 58 76 69 64

See how none of them are near 100?

- Bob

This kind of model is referred to as a “intractable likelihood” model in
the statistics literature and it cannot be done in Stan.  The problem is
computing that normalizing term — the only way to we know how to
compute high-dimensional intervals accurately is MCMC!  There are
Sequential Monte Carlo approaches that formally give an answer,
but they can be difficult to scale to the scope of these problems.

Ultimately this is a screaming application of the “Folk Theorem”. 
You probably don’t want to built this model but rather another model
that doesn’t integrate out the marginalized parameters at all and instead
tries to fit everything jointly.

On Jan 14, 2017, at 8:06 AM, Samuel Hinton <samue...@gmail.com> wrote:

As to what I am unable to put into stan, it is a high dimensional integral that appears on the denominator of the likelihood, not the numerator, so the standard way of marginalising over parameters doesn't won't work. If there is a way to put a theta-dependent integral on the denominator of the joint lpdf I would be very happy to break free of my ignorance!
